title: Patatas Bravas
shortDescription: Crispy fried potatoes served with spicy tomato sauce and garlicky aioli, part of a tapas trio with Gambas al Ajillo and Pan con Tomate.
note: Cut potatoes into uniform 1-inch cubes and double-fry for maximum crispiness.
introCopy: Patatas bravas are one of Spain's most iconic tapas. The name means 'fierce potatoes,' a nod to the spicy sauce that coats them. This Madrid classic is essential bar food.

steps.text: Make the bravas sauce: heat olive oil, cook garlic 1 minute, stir in paprika, cayenne, tomatoes, and salt; simmer 10 minutes until thickened.
Make the aioli by whisking mayonnaise, garlic, and lemon juice together; refrigerate.
Fry potatoes in 325°F oil for 6-8 minutes until tender but pale; drain.
Raise oil to 375°F and fry potatoes again for 3-4 minutes until deeply golden and crisp; drain and salt.
Plate potatoes, drizzle with bravas sauce and aioli, and serve at once.

title: Gambas al Ajillo
shortDescription: Sizzling garlic shrimp cooked in olive oil with dried chiles, served bubbling hot with bread, part of a tapas trio with Patatas Bravas and Pan con Tomate.
note: Don't overcook the shrimp; they need just 2-3 minutes to turn pink and tender.
introCopy: Gambas al ajillo is a quintessential Andalusian tapa, arriving at the table still sizzling in its cazuela. The garlicky, chile-spiked olive oil is meant to be mopped up with crusty bread.

steps.text: Pat shrimp dry and season with salt.
Heat olive oil in a skillet over medium heat; add garlic and peppers and cook until fragrant and just golden, about 2 minutes.
Add shrimp and paprika; cook, stirring, until shrimp are just pink and cooked through, 2-3 minutes.
Remove from heat, scatter with parsley, and serve immediately with bread for dipping.

title: Pan con Tomate
shortDescription: Crispy toasted bread rubbed with garlic and ripe tomato, finished with fruity olive oil, part of a tapas trio with Patatas Bravas and Gambas al Ajillo.
note: Use the ripest, juiciest tomatoes you can find; the pulp should grate easily against the bread.
introCopy: Pa amb tomàquet is Catalonia's most beloved preparation, a deceptively simple combination of toasted bread, tomato, garlic, and olive oil served at nearly every meal. It's the perfect canvas for Spain's finest ingredients.

steps.text: Toast or grill bread slices until golden and crisp on both sides.
While bread is warm, rub one side with the cut garlic clove.
Rub the cut side of the tomato over the bread, pressing to release pulp and juice; discard the skin.
Drizzle generously with olive oil, sprinkle with sea salt, and serve at once.

title: Croquetas de Jamón
shortDescription: Golden, crispy fried croquettes with a creamy béchamel and Serrano ham filling, part of a tapas trio with Tortilla Española and Pimientos de Padrón.
note: Chill the béchamel thoroughly, even overnight, so the croquetas hold their shape when fried.
introCopy: Croquetas de jamón are found on nearly every tapas bar menu in Spain. A silky ham-studded béchamel is chilled, breaded, and fried until the outside shatters to reveal a molten center.

steps.text: Melt butter in a saucepan, cook onion until soft, about 5 minutes.
Whisk in flour and cook 2 minutes to form a roux, stirring constantly.
Gradually whisk in warm milk, cooking until very thick, about 10 minutes; stir in ham, nutmeg, and salt.
Spread mixture into a dish, cover, and chill at least 2 hours or overnight.
Shape chilled mixture into small logs; dredge in flour, egg, then breadcrumbs.
Fry in 350°F oil in batches until deep golden, about 3 minutes; drain and serve hot.

title: Tortilla Española
shortDescription: A thick, tender Spanish omelet of slow-cooked potatoes, onions, and eggs, part of a tapas trio with Croquetas de Jamón and Pimientos de Padrón.
note: Cook the potatoes low and slow in the oil so they turn tender, not crispy, before adding the eggs.
introCopy: Tortilla española, or tortilla de patatas, is Spain's beloved potato omelet found in every home and bar. Served warm or at room temperature, it's equally at home as tapas, a light lunch, or a sandwich filling.

steps.text: Heat olive oil in a wide skillet over medium-low heat. Add potatoes and onion, season with salt, and cook gently, turning occasionally, until tender but not browned, 20-25 minutes.
Drain potatoes and onion in a colander over a bowl, reserving the oil.
Beat eggs in a large bowl with remaining salt, then fold in the warm potatoes and onion.
Heat 2 tbsp of the reserved oil in a nonstick skillet over medium heat. Pour in the mixture and cook until the edges set, about 4 minutes.
Place a plate over the skillet, flip the tortilla onto it, then slide back into the pan to cook the other side, about 3-4 minutes, until just set in the center.
Slide onto a plate and let rest 5 minutes before slicing into wedges.

title: Pimientos de Padrón
shortDescription: Blistered small green peppers fried in olive oil and finished with flaky salt, part of a tapas trio with Croquetas de Jamón and Tortilla Española.
note: A few peppers in every batch are surprisingly spicy — that's part of the fun, according to the Galician saying.
introCopy: Pimientos de Padrón hail from the Galician town of Padrón and are a beloved tapas bar staple. Fried quickly in hot oil until blistered, they're the ultimate simple snack, though a hidden spicy one occasionally surprises you.

steps.text: Rinse peppers and pat completely dry.
Heat olive oil in a large skillet over high heat until shimmering.
Add peppers in a single layer and fry, turning occasionally, until blistered and softened, about 5-7 minutes.
Transfer to a plate, sprinkle generously with flaky salt, and serve immediately.

title: Boquerones en Vinagre
shortDescription: Fresh anchovies marinated in vinegar, olive oil, and garlic until silky and tangy, part of a tapas trio with Albóndigas en Salsa de Almendras and Champiñones al Ajillo.
note: Freeze the anchovies for 48 hours before marinating to eliminate any parasite risk, a standard practice for this raw-cured dish.
introCopy: Boquerones en vinagre are fresh anchovies cured in vinegar rather than salt, giving them a delicate, tangy flavor completely different from tinned anchovies. They're a refreshing, bright staple of Spanish tapas bars.

ingredients.prepNote: cleaned, butterflied, and frozen 48 hours, then thawed

steps.text: Arrange anchovy fillets in a single layer in a shallow dish.
Whisk together vinegar, water, and salt; pour over anchovies, ensuring they're fully submerged.
Cover and refrigerate 4-6 hours, until the flesh turns opaque white.
Drain the anchovies, discarding the marinade. Arrange on a plate, scatter with garlic and parsley, and drizzle with olive oil.
Chill 30 minutes before serving to let the flavors meld.

title: Albóndigas en Salsa de Almendras
shortDescription: Tender pork and beef meatballs simmered in a rich almond and saffron sauce, part of a tapas trio with Boquerones en Vinagre and Champiñones al Ajillo.
note: Toast the almonds before grinding them into the sauce for deeper, nuttier flavor.
introCopy: These Spanish meatballs in almond sauce showcase the Moorish influence on Spanish cooking, with saffron and toasted almonds thickening a fragrant sauce. They're a hearty, comforting tapa perfect for sopping up with bread.

steps.text: Combine meatball ingredients in a bowl and mix gently; form into 1-inch balls.
Heat 2 tbsp olive oil in a large skillet and brown meatballs on all sides, about 6 minutes; remove and set aside.
In the same pan, add remaining oil and cook onion until soft, about 5 minutes.
Blend toasted almonds, garlic, and saffron with a splash of stock into a coarse paste; stir into the onions along with remaining stock and wine.
Return meatballs to the pan, cover, and simmer gently until sauce thickens and meatballs are cooked through, about 20 minutes.

title: Champiñones al Ajillo
shortDescription: Mushrooms sautéed in olive oil with garlic, sherry, and parsley, part of a tapas trio with Boquerones en Vinagre and Albóndigas en Salsa de Almendras.
note: Don't crowd the pan — sauté mushrooms in batches if needed so they brown rather than steam.
introCopy: Champiñones al ajillo is a simple but deeply savory tapa found across Spain. Earthy mushrooms soak up garlicky, sherry-spiked olive oil, best mopped up with crusty bread.

steps.text: Heat olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat.
Add mushrooms in a single layer and cook without stirring for 3-4 minutes until browned on one side.
Add garlic and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 1 minute.
Pour in sherry and cook until evaporated, about 1 minute; season with salt.
Remove from heat, stir in parsley, and serve immediately with bread.

title: Paella Valenciana
shortDescription: The original saffron rice dish from Valencia with chicken, rabbit, green beans, and lima beans cooked in a wide shallow pan.
note: Resist stirring the rice once the liquid is added — this allows the prized crispy socarrat to form on the bottom.
introCopy: Paella Valenciana is the authentic ancestor of all paellas, born in the rice fields outside Valencia. Traditionalists insist on chicken, rabbit, and local beans rather than seafood, cooked over an open flame in a wide paellera.

ingredients.prepNote: cut into pieces, or additional chicken

steps.text: Heat olive oil in a paellera over medium-high heat. Brown chicken and rabbit pieces well on all sides, about 10 minutes; push to the edges.
Add green beans and lima beans to the center and cook 5 minutes, then stir in grated tomato and paprika, cooking until thickened, 5 minutes.
Sprinkle rice evenly over the pan and stir briefly to coat in the sofrito.
Pour in hot stock infused with saffron, add rosemary and salt, and stir once to distribute evenly.
Simmer uncovered without stirring for 18-20 minutes, until rice is tender and liquid is absorbed, raising heat for the last 2 minutes to form socarrat.
Remove from heat, cover with a towel, and rest 5 minutes before serving with lemon wedges.

title: Paella de Marisco
shortDescription: A vibrant seafood paella loaded with shrimp, mussels, clams, and squid in a saffron-infused rice base.
note: Add delicate seafood like shrimp toward the end of cooking to prevent it from turning rubbery.
introCopy: Paella de marisco swaps the meats of the original for the bounty of the Mediterranean and Atlantic coasts. Shrimp, mussels, clams, and squid make this the showstopping seafood version beloved in coastal Spain.

steps.text: Heat oil in a paellera over medium heat; cook onion and garlic until soft, about 5 minutes.
Add tomato and cook until reduced and jammy, about 8 minutes.
Stir in rice and saffron, coating in the sofrito, then pour in hot stock and salt.
Simmer uncovered 10 minutes, then nestle squid, mussels, and clams into the rice.
Continue cooking 8 minutes, adding shrimp for the final 5 minutes, until rice is tender and shellfish have opened.
Rest 5 minutes off heat, discard any unopened shells, and serve with lemon wedges.

title: Arroz Negro
shortDescription: Dramatic squid ink rice studded with tender squid and shrimp, traditionally served with a dollop of garlicky alioli.
note: Squeeze the ink sacs carefully into a small bowl of stock before mixing in to avoid losing any precious ink.
introCopy: Arroz negro, or black rice, gets its striking color and briny depth from squid ink. A Catalan and Valencian specialty, it's traditionally topped with a spoonful of alioli that melts into the rice.

steps.text: Heat olive oil in a paellera; cook onion and pepper until soft, about 6 minutes, then add garlic and tomato and cook until jammy, 6 minutes.
Add squid and cook 3 minutes, then stir in rice, coating well in the sofrito.
Whisk squid ink into the hot stock, then pour over the rice along with salt.
Simmer uncovered 15 minutes without stirring, adding shrimp for the last 5 minutes, until rice is tender.
Rest 5 minutes, then serve with dollops of alioli.

title: Fideuà
shortDescription: A Valencian noodle paella made with short toasted pasta instead of rice, packed with shrimp, squid, and monkfish.
note: Toast the noodles in oil before adding stock; this gives them a nutty flavor and helps them hold their shape.
introCopy: Fideuà is Valencia's answer to paella, using short, thin noodles instead of rice. Legend says it was invented by a fisherman's cook who ran out of rice. It's traditionally served with alioli on the side.

steps.text: Heat 2 tbsp oil in a wide paellera; toast noodles over medium heat, stirring often, until golden brown, about 5 minutes. Remove and set aside.
Add remaining oil, cook onion and garlic until soft, then add tomato and cook until jammy, about 8 minutes.
Add monkfish and squid, cooking 3 minutes, then return noodles to the pan and stir to coat.
Pour in hot stock infused with saffron and salt; simmer uncovered 10 minutes.
Nestle shrimp into the noodles and cook 5 more minutes, until noodles are tender and liquid absorbed.
Rest 5 minutes and serve with alioli.

title: Cocido Madrileño
shortDescription: A hearty Madrid chickpea stew simmered with beef, chorizo, morcilla, and vegetables, traditionally served in three courses.
note: Traditionally the broth is served first as soup, then the chickpeas and vegetables, and finally the meats — but it's equally delicious served all together.
introCopy: Cocido madrileño is the ultimate Spanish comfort stew, a slow-simmered pot of chickpeas, meats, and vegetables that has fed Madrid families for centuries. It's a full meal in one pot, traditionally stretched across three courses.

steps.text: In a very large pot, combine soaked chickpeas, beef, chicken, pork belly, ham bone, onion, and water. Bring to a boil, skimming off foam.
Reduce heat and simmer gently, partially covered, for 2 hours, until chickpeas and meats are tender.
Add carrots, potatoes, chorizo, and morcilla; simmer 30 more minutes.
Add cabbage wedges and cook a final 15 minutes; season broth with salt.
Strain some broth into a separate pot, add fideos, and simmer 5 minutes to serve as a first course soup.
Serve the chickpeas and vegetables, and the sliced meats, as subsequent courses.

title: Fabada Asturiana
shortDescription: A rich white bean stew from Asturias simmered with chorizo, morcilla, and pork shoulder until deeply savory.
note: Use large, creamy fabes beans if you can find them — their thin skins make for an especially silky stew.
introCopy: Fabada asturiana is the signature dish of Spain's rainy northern coast, a soul-warming stew of large white beans and smoky pork. It's traditionally eaten slowly with crusty bread on a cold day.

steps.text: Drain soaked beans and place in a large pot with pork shoulder, pancetta, onion, garlic, and bay leaves. Cover with water.
Bring to a gentle boil, skimming off foam, then reduce heat and simmer very gently for 1.5 hours, adding a splash of cold water occasionally to keep beans tender ('assustar las fabes').
Add chorizo and morcilla, and simmer 45 more minutes until beans are creamy and meats are tender.
Stir in saffron and salt during the last 15 minutes.
Remove onion, garlic, and bay leaves. Let rest 10 minutes before serving, slicing sausages for serving.

title: Marmitako
shortDescription: A rustic Basque fisherman's stew of fresh tuna, potatoes, and peppers in a smoky tomato broth.
note: Break the potatoes apart rather than slicing cleanly — this releases starch that naturally thickens the broth.
introCopy: Marmitako takes its name from the marmita, the pot Basque fishermen used to cook tuna caught fresh at sea. Chunks of tuna are simmered briefly with potatoes and peppers for a simple, deeply satisfying one-pot meal.

steps.text: Heat olive oil in a pot and cook onion and peppers until soft, about 8 minutes.
Add garlic, tomato, and paprika; cook until jammy, about 6 minutes.
Add potatoes and stock, bring to a boil, then simmer until potatoes are tender, about 20 minutes.
Season with salt, add tuna chunks, and simmer gently just until cooked through, 3-4 minutes (do not overcook).
Remove from heat, stir in parsley, and let rest 5 minutes before serving.

title: Rabo de Toro
shortDescription: Andalusian oxtail slow-braised in red wine with vegetables until falling off the bone and deeply rich.
note: This dish tastes even better the next day, once the sauce has had time to meld and any fat has been skimmed off the chilled surface.
introCopy: Rabo de toro originated in Córdoba, tied to the region's bullfighting tradition, though today it's simply beloved as a rich, wine-braised oxtail stew. Long, slow cooking transforms this tough cut into meltingly tender comfort food.

steps.text: Season oxtail with salt. Heat olive oil in a Dutch oven and brown oxtail well on all sides, in batches; set aside.
Add carrots, onion, and celery to the pot and cook until softened, about 8 minutes; add garlic and cook 1 minute.
Pour in wine, scraping up browned bits, and simmer 5 minutes to reduce slightly.
Return oxtail to the pot, add tomatoes, stock, bay leaves, and peppercorns. Bring to a simmer, cover, and cook low for 3 hours, until meat is falling off the bone.
Skim excess fat, remove bay leaves, and adjust seasoning. Serve over mashed potatoes.

title: Callos a la Madrileña
shortDescription: A robust Madrid tripe stew simmered with chorizo, morcilla, and paprika until rich and gelatinous.
note: Blanch the tripe thoroughly before the main cook to remove any strong odor and ensure a clean flavor.
introCopy: Callos a la madrileña is a beloved winter dish in Madrid's tascas, transforming humble tripe into a deeply savory, paprika-spiced stew. It's an acquired taste for some, but a nostalgic classic for many Spaniards.

steps.text: Blanch tripe in boiling water for 5 minutes, then drain and rinse well.
Place tripe in a large pot with the whole onion and bay leaves, cover with water, and simmer gently 2 hours until tender.
In a separate pan, heat olive oil and cook diced onion and garlic until soft, about 6 minutes; add chorizo and morcilla and cook 3 minutes.
Stir in both paprikas and crushed tomatoes; simmer 10 minutes.
Drain tripe (reserving some cooking liquid) and add to the sauce along with enough reserved liquid to loosen. Simmer 30 minutes, seasoning with salt.

title: Pisto Manchego
shortDescription: A slow-cooked medley of zucchini, peppers, onion, and tomato from La Mancha, similar to ratatouille but distinctly Spanish.
note: Cook the vegetables separately before combining to avoid a watery pisto — this preserves their individual textures.
introCopy: Pisto manchego hails from the plains of La Mancha and is often topped with a fried egg for a simple, satisfying meal. This vegetable stew celebrates summer's bounty, cooked low and slow until silky and sweet.

steps.text: Heat olive oil in a large skillet; cook onion and peppers until softened, about 10 minutes.
Add zucchini and garlic; cook another 8 minutes until zucchini softens.
Stir in tomatoes, sugar, and salt; simmer uncovered, stirring occasionally, until thick and jammy, about 20 minutes.
Serve warm as is, or topped with a fried egg.

title: Pulpo a la Gallega
shortDescription: Tender octopus sliced over paprika-dusted potatoes, drizzled generously with olive oil, a signature dish of Galicia.
note: Dipping the octopus into boiling water three times before fully submerging it helps keep the skin from splitting as it cooks.
introCopy: Pulpo a la gallega is Galicia's most famous dish, traditionally served on a wooden plate at pulperías. Perfectly tender octopus meets earthy potatoes and smoky paprika in a dish that's deceptively simple yet deeply flavorful.

steps.text: Bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil. Holding the octopus by the head, dip it into the water 3 times, letting the legs curl, then submerge fully.
Reduce to a simmer and cook octopus, covered, until fork-tender, about 45-50 minutes.
Meanwhile, boil potatoes in salted water until tender, about 20 minutes; drain and slice into rounds.
Remove octopus and let rest 5 minutes, then slice tentacles into thick rounds.
Arrange potato slices on a wooden board or plate, top with octopus, drizzle generously with olive oil, and dust with paprika and salt.

title: Zarzuela de Mariscos
shortDescription: A festive Catalan seafood stew combining fish, shrimp, clams, and mussels in a saffron and almond-thickened sauce.
note: Use the freshest seafood you can find and add each type at a different time so nothing overcooks.
introCopy: Zarzuela de mariscos takes its name from the lively Spanish musical theater form, reflecting the dish's vibrant mix of seafood. This celebratory stew from Catalonia brings together the best of the sea in one fragrant pot.

steps.text: Heat olive oil in a wide pot; cook onion and pepper until soft, 8 minutes. Add garlic and tomato, cooking until jammy, 8 minutes.
Pour in wine and reduce by half, then add fish stock and bring to a simmer.
Blend picada ingredients (almonds, garlic, saffron, parsley) with a splash of stock into a paste; stir into the pot.
Add white fish and shrimp, simmer 3 minutes, then add mussels and clams; cover and cook until shells open, about 6-8 minutes.
Season with salt, discard any unopened shells, and serve immediately with crusty bread.

title: Bacalao al Pil Pil
shortDescription: Basque salt cod gently poached in olive oil and emulsified into a silky, garlicky sauce using only the fish's natural gelatin.
note: Keep the heat very low and swirl the pan constantly — the sauce emulsifies from the collagen in the cod skin, not from any thickener.
introCopy: Bacalao al pil pil is a Basque masterpiece of technique over ingredients, transforming just cod, garlic, and olive oil into a luxuriously creamy sauce through patient emulsification. It's considered one of the pinnacles of Basque cuisine.

steps.text: Pat desalinated cod fillets dry with paper towels.
Heat olive oil in a wide shallow pan over low heat; gently fry garlic and chile until golden, then remove and reserve.
Add cod skin-side down to the warm (not hot) oil and cook very gently over low heat for about 10 minutes, without browning.

Remove the pan from heat and, tilting it gently, swirl the oil in a circular motion, gradually working in small movements to emulsify the released gelatin into a creamy sauce; return briefly to low heat if it separates.
Once thickened and creamy, return the fried garlic on top and serve immediately.

title: Merluza en Salsa Verde
shortDescription: Hake fillets gently poached in a vibrant green sauce of parsley, garlic, white wine, and clams.
note: Shake the pan gently rather than stirring to help the sauce emulsify without breaking apart the delicate fish.
introCopy: Merluza en salsa verde is a Basque country classic showcasing hake, one of Spain's most prized fish. The bright green herb sauce, studded with clams, is a testament to the region's mastery of delicate seafood cookery.

steps.text: Season hake with salt. Heat olive oil in a wide pan and sauté garlic until fragrant, 1 minute.
Sprinkle in flour and stir 1 minute, then pour in wine and stock, whisking to combine.
Stir in half the parsley and bring to a gentle simmer.
Nestle hake fillets and clams into the sauce; cover and cook gently, shaking the pan occasionally, until fish is just cooked and clams have opened, about 8-10 minutes.
Sprinkle with remaining parsley and serve immediately with the sauce spooned over.

title: Calamares a la Romana
shortDescription: Crispy fried squid rings in a light batter, served with lemon wedges and alioli — a beloved bar snack across Spain.
note: Fry in small batches so the oil temperature doesn't drop, keeping the coating light and crisp rather than greasy.
introCopy: Despite the name referencing Rome, calamares a la romana is a beloved Spanish tapas bar staple. Tender squid rings get a light flour dredge and quick fry, resulting in an irresistibly crisp bite best enjoyed piping hot.

steps.text: Pat squid rings very dry with paper towels.
Combine flour, salt, and pepper in a shallow bowl.
Heat oil in a deep pot to 375°F.
Dredge squid rings in seasoned flour, shaking off excess, and fry in batches for 1.5-2 minutes until golden and crisp.
Drain on paper towels and serve immediately with lemon wedges and alioli.

title: Mejillones a la Marinera
shortDescription: Plump mussels steamed in a garlicky white wine and tomato broth, ready to eat with bread in under 20 minutes.
note: Discard any mussels that don't close when tapped before cooking, and any that remain closed after cooking.
introCopy: Mejillones a la marinera, or sailor-style mussels, is a simple coastal classic found from Galicia to the Mediterranean. The briny, garlicky broth is just as delicious as the mussels themselves.

steps.text: Heat olive oil in a large pot; cook onion until soft, about 5 minutes, then add garlic and cook 1 minute.
Stir in grated tomato and paprika, cooking until slightly reduced, about 4 minutes.
Pour in wine and bring to a simmer.
Add mussels, cover, and cook, shaking the pot occasionally, until shells open, about 5-6 minutes.
Discard any unopened mussels, stir in parsley, and serve immediately with bread.

title: Vieiras Gratinadas
shortDescription: Galician scallops baked in their shells with a golden breadcrumb, garlic, and Jerez ham topping.
note: Serve the scallops in their scrubbed shells for an authentic presentation, as they do in Galician marisquerías.
introCopy: Vieiras gratinadas showcase Galicia's famous scallops, prized enough to become the symbol of the Camino de Santiago pilgrimage. A savory breadcrumb topping and quick broil bring out their natural sweetness.

steps.text: Preheat broiler. Heat olive oil in a skillet; cook onion until soft, about 5 minutes, then add garlic and ham and cook 2 minutes.
Sear scallops briefly, about 1 minute per side, just to color; remove and set aside.
Stir breadcrumbs and parsley into the onion mixture; toss with melted butter and salt.
Place scallops in shells or a baking dish, top each with the breadcrumb mixture.
Broil until golden and bubbling, about 3-4 minutes. Serve immediately.

title: Huevos Rotos con Jamón
shortDescription: Crispy fried potatoes topped with Serrano ham and broken fried eggs, the yolks mingling into a rich sauce.
note: Fry the eggs so the whites are crisp at the edges but the yolks stay runny — breaking them tableside is part of the tradition.
introCopy: Huevos rotos, meaning 'broken eggs,' is a modern Madrid tapas classic. Crispy potatoes are piled high, draped with Serrano ham, and crowned with fried eggs that are broken to let the golden yolk cascade over everything.

ingredients.prepNote: peeled and cut into thick fries

steps.text: Heat olive oil in a deep skillet to 325°F. Fry potatoes until tender, about 8 minutes; remove and drain.
Raise oil to 375°F and fry potatoes again until golden and crisp, about 4 minutes; drain and salt.
In a separate pan, fry eggs in a little olive oil until whites are crisp at the edges and yolks remain runny, about 3 minutes.
Pile crispy potatoes onto plates, drape with Serrano ham, and top with fried eggs.
Break the egg yolks over the top just before serving so they run into the potatoes.

title: Revuelto de Setas
shortDescription: Soft, silky scrambled eggs folded with sautéed wild mushrooms and garlic, a beloved autumn tapa.
note: Cook the eggs over low heat and remove from the pan while still slightly underdone — they'll continue cooking in the residual heat.
introCopy: Revuelto de setas celebrates the wild mushroom season in Spain's forests, especially popular in the north. Softly scrambled eggs are the perfect match for earthy, garlicky mushrooms, often finished with a touch of Serrano ham.

steps.text: Heat olive oil in a skillet over medium-high heat; sauté mushrooms until golden and any liquid has evaporated, about 7 minutes.
Add garlic and cook 1 minute until fragrant.
Lower heat, season with salt, and pour in beaten eggs.
Gently stir eggs with a spatula over low heat until softly set and creamy, about 3 minutes.
Scatter with parsley and serve immediately with bread.

title: Crema Catalana
shortDescription: A silky citrus and cinnamon-infused custard topped with a brittle caramelized sugar crust, Catalonia's answer to crème brûlée.
note: Use a wide, shallow dish for each serving so you get maximum surface area of crackly caramelized sugar.
introCopy: Crema catalana predates its French cousin crème brûlée by centuries and is traditionally served on Saint Joseph's Day. The custard is infused with lemon and orange zest and cinnamon, then topped with a torched sugar shell just before serving.

steps.text: Heat milk with cinnamon stick and citrus zests in a saucepan until just simmering; remove from heat and let steep 15 minutes, then strain.
Whisk egg yolks with 3/4 cup sugar and cornstarch until pale and smooth.
Gradually whisk warm milk into the egg mixture, then return to the saucepan.
Cook over medium-low heat, stirring constantly, until thickened enough to coat the back of a spoon, about 8-10 minutes.
Pour into shallow ramekins and refrigerate at least 3 hours, until fully set.
Just before serving, sprinkle a thin layer of sugar over each custard and caramelize with a kitchen torch until crackly and golden.

title: Churros con Chocolate
shortDescription: Crispy, ridged fried dough dusted with cinnamon sugar, served with a cup of thick, rich drinking chocolate for dipping.
note: Pipe the dough directly into the hot oil for the classic ridged shape, using a star-tipped piping bag or churrera.
introCopy: Churros con chocolate is a beloved Spanish breakfast and late-night treat, enjoyed at churrerías from Madrid to Seville. The crunchy, cinnamon-dusted dough is made for dunking into thick, almost pudding-like hot chocolate.

steps.text: Combine water, sugar, salt, and olive oil in a saucepan and bring to a boil.
Remove from heat and stir in flour vigorously until a smooth dough forms; let cool slightly.
Transfer dough to a piping bag fitted with a star tip. Heat frying oil to 375°F.
Pipe 4-inch lengths directly into the hot oil, frying a few at a time until golden, about 3-4 minutes; drain and roll in cinnamon sugar.
For the chocolate, whisk cornstarch into a splash of cold milk. Heat remaining milk with chocolate until melted, then stir in cornstarch slurry and cook until thickened, about 5 minutes.
Serve warm churros alongside cups of hot chocolate for dipping.

title: Tarta de Santiago
shortDescription: A dense, moist Galician almond cake flavored with lemon zest and dusted with powdered sugar in the shape of the Cross of Saint James.
note: Use a stencil of the Cross of Santiago when dusting with powdered sugar for the traditional decorative finish.
introCopy: Tarta de Santiago is a centuries-old Galician cake tied to the pilgrimage route to Santiago de Compostela. Made simply from ground almonds, eggs, and sugar with no flour, it has a naturally moist, rich crumb.

steps.text: Preheat oven to 350°F and butter a 9-inch round cake pan.
Whisk eggs and sugar together until pale and slightly thickened, about 3 minutes.
Stir in almond flour, lemon zest, cinnamon, and almond extract until well combined.
Pour batter into the prepared pan and bake until golden and a toothpick comes out clean, about 30-35 minutes.
Cool completely in the pan, then dust generously with powdered sugar before serving.

title: Flan de Huevo
shortDescription: A classic silky egg custard topped with a pool of golden caramel, unmolded to reveal its glossy amber cap.
note: Run a thin knife around the edge of the flan before unmolding to help release it cleanly onto the plate.
introCopy: Flan is a beloved dessert throughout Spain, a simple baked custard crowned with deep caramel. Cooked gently in a water bath, it emerges silky smooth, and the caramel forms a natural sauce once unmolded.

steps.text: Preheat oven to 325°F. Make the caramel by heating sugar and water in a saucepan over medium heat until deep amber, without stirring; immediately pour into a 9-inch round baking dish or individual ramekins, tilting to coat.
Whisk eggs, egg yolks, and sugar together until smooth.
Heat milk and cream until just warm, then gradually whisk into the egg mixture along with vanilla.
Strain custard through a fine sieve into the caramel-lined dish.
Place in a larger pan, add hot water halfway up the sides, and bake until just set with a slight jiggle in the center, about 40-45 minutes.
Cool completely, then refrigerate at least 4 hours. Invert onto a plate to unmold before serving.

title: Turrón Helado
shortDescription: A frozen almond nougat parfait inspired by traditional turrón, studded with toasted almonds and honey.
note: Toast the almonds until deeply golden for the best nutty flavor to contrast with the sweet, creamy base.
introCopy: Turrón helado transforms Spain's beloved Christmas almond nougat into a frozen semifreddo-style dessert. It captures all the honeyed, nutty flavor of traditional turrón in a cool, creamy, make-ahead form perfect for entertaining.

steps.text: Line a loaf pan with plastic wrap, leaving overhang on the sides.
Whisk egg whites in a heatproof bowl set over simmering water with honey until warm and doubled in volume, about 5 minutes; remove and whip until cool and glossy, forming stiff peaks.
In a separate bowl, whip cream with powdered sugar and vanilla to soft peaks.
Gently fold whipped cream into the meringue, then fold in toasted almonds and cinnamon.
Pour into the prepared pan, smooth the top, and freeze at least 6 hours or overnight until firm.
Unmold, slice, and serve frozen.

title: Torrijas
shortDescription: Thick slices of bread soaked in cinnamon-spiced milk, fried until golden, and finished with a honey glaze — Spain's take on French toast.
note: Use slightly stale bread so it soaks up the milk without falling apart during frying.
introCopy: Torrijas are a beloved Easter and Lent tradition in Spain, dating back centuries as a way to use up day-old bread. Soaked in sweet spiced milk and fried until golden, they're finished with honey or sugar for an irresistible treat.

steps.text: Heat milk with sugar, cinnamon stick, and lemon zest until just simmering; remove from heat and let cool slightly.
Strain milk into a shallow dish. Soak bread slices in the milk for 1-2 minutes per side, until softened but still holding together.
Dip soaked bread slices in beaten egg, coating both sides.
Heat olive oil in a skillet over medium heat; fry bread slices until golden brown, about 2-3 minutes per side.
Drain briefly, then toss in cinnamon sugar while still warm and drizzle with honey if using.

title: Gazpacho Andaluz
shortDescription: A refreshing chilled soup of ripe tomatoes, cucumber, pepper, and garlic blended silky smooth with olive oil and sherry vinegar.
note: Chill the soup for at least 2 hours before serving — gazpacho tastes best ice cold on a hot day.
introCopy: Gazpacho andaluz is southern Spain's answer to summer heat, a vibrant blended soup that requires no cooking at all. Ripe tomatoes and a splash of sherry vinegar give it a bright, refreshing tang that's endlessly craveable.

steps.text: Combine tomatoes, cucumber, pepper, onion, garlic, and bread in a blender.
Blend until smooth, then with the motor running, drizzle in olive oil and vinegar.
Season with salt and blend again; pass through a fine sieve for extra silkiness if desired.
Refrigerate at least 2 hours until well chilled.
Serve cold in bowls, topped with diced vegetable garnish if using.

title: Salmorejo Cordobés
shortDescription: A thick, creamy chilled tomato and bread soup from Córdoba, topped with chopped hard-boiled egg and Serrano ham.
note: Use very ripe, high-quality tomatoes since they're the star flavor of this simple, unadulterated soup.
introCopy: Salmorejo cordobés is thicker and creamier than gazpacho, blending tomatoes and bread with a generous amount of olive oil until velvety. It's traditionally topped with diced hard-boiled egg and ham for texture and richness.

steps.text: Blend tomatoes, bread, and garlic together until smooth.
With the motor running, slowly drizzle in olive oil until the mixture is thick and emulsified.
Stir in vinegar and salt; blend once more, then pass through a fine sieve for a silky texture.
Refrigerate at least 2 hours until well chilled.
Serve in bowls topped with chopped egg and diced Serrano ham, with a drizzle of olive oil.

title: Ajoblanco
shortDescription: A silky chilled almond and garlic soup from Málaga, traditionally garnished with sweet grapes or melon for contrast.
note: Soak the almonds and bread in water beforehand for an extra-smooth, creamy consistency.
introCopy: Ajoblanco predates gazpacho and is considered one of Spain's oldest cold soups, rooted in Moorish culinary traditions. Ground almonds and garlic are blended with bread and olive oil, traditionally finished with a scattering of sweet grapes.

ingredients.prepNote: crust removed, torn and soaked in water

steps.text: Drain soaked almonds and bread, and combine in a blender with garlic and a splash of the cold water.
Blend until very smooth, several minutes, scraping down as needed.
With the motor running, drizzle in olive oil until emulsified and creamy.
Add vinegar, salt, and remaining water; blend until silky smooth. Adjust consistency with more water if needed.
Refrigerate at least 2 hours until well chilled, then serve topped with halved grapes.

title: Escalivada
shortDescription: Smoky roasted eggplant, red peppers, and onions dressed simply with olive oil, a beloved Catalan vegetable dish served at room temperature.
note: Let the vegetables steam in a covered bowl after roasting — this makes peeling the skins away much easier.
introCopy: Escalivada means 'cooked in ashes' in Catalan, referencing its origins of being roasted directly over embers. Today it's typically oven-roasted, resulting in silky, smoky vegetables that are equally good as a side or piled onto bread.

steps.text: Preheat oven to 425°F. Place whole eggplants, peppers, and onions on a baking sheet.
Roast, turning occasionally, until vegetables are completely soft and charred in spots, about 40-45 minutes (removing peppers earlier if they finish first).
Transfer vegetables to a bowl, cover with plastic wrap, and let steam for 15 minutes.
Peel away skins, seeds, and stems, then tear the flesh into strips by hand.
Arrange on a platter, drizzle with olive oil, sprinkle with garlic if using and salt, and serve at room temperature.

title: Cochinillo Asado
shortDescription: Whole roast suckling pig from Segovia with impossibly crackling skin and tender, succulent meat, traditionally carved with the edge of a plate.
note: Basting periodically with the pan juices and rendered fat is essential for achieving that famous shattering crackling skin.
introCopy: Cochinillo asado is Segovia's most famous dish, a whole suckling pig roasted low and slow until the skin turns impossibly crisp. Legend has it the meat should be so tender it can be carved with the edge of a plate.

steps.text: Preheat oven to 350°F. Rub the pig inside and out with lard, salt, pepper, and crushed garlic; place bay leaves inside the cavity.
Place skin-side up on a large roasting rack, pour wine into the pan, and roast for about 2.5 hours, basting occasionally with pan juices.
Increase oven temperature to 450°F for the final 20-30 minutes to crisp the skin until deeply golden and crackling.
Let rest 15 minutes before carving, traditionally using the edge of a plate to demonstrate tenderness.

title: Empanada Gallega
shortDescription: A large savory Galician pie filled with tuna, peppers, onions, and tomato sauce, encased in a golden, slightly chewy crust.
note: Cut a few small vents in the top crust to let steam escape and prevent the empanada from becoming soggy.
introCopy: Empanada gallega is a beloved Galician staple, a substantial savory pie traditionally filled with tuna or seafood in a rich sofrito. It's served at room temperature, sliced into squares, at celebrations and everyday lunches alike.

steps.text: Dissolve yeast in warm water; combine with flour, olive oil, and salt, kneading into a smooth dough. Cover and let rise 1 hour.
Meanwhile, heat olive oil and cook onions and peppers slowly until very soft and sweet, about 25 minutes.
Stir in tomato and paprika, cooking until thick and jammy, about 15 minutes; fold in tuna and salt, then cool completely.
Divide dough in half and roll each into a rectangle. Place one on a baking sheet, spread filling evenly, and top with the second sheet, crimping edges to seal.
Brush with beaten egg, cut a few vents in the top, and bake at 400°F until deep golden, about 35-40 minutes.
Cool slightly before slicing into squares and serving.

title: Arroz con Leche
shortDescription: Creamy Spanish rice pudding slowly simmered in milk with cinnamon and lemon zest, served warm or chilled with a dusting of cinnamon.
note: Stir frequently while the rice simmers to prevent it from sticking and to build the pudding's signature creaminess.
introCopy: Arroz con leche is a comforting dessert enjoyed across Spain, particularly beloved in Asturias where it's practically a regional symbol. Simple pantry ingredients transform into a rich, fragrant pudding through patient, slow simmering.

steps.text: Combine rice, water, cinnamon stick, and lemon zest in a saucepan; bring to a boil and simmer 5 minutes.
Add milk and salt, reduce heat to low, and simmer gently, stirring often, for 30-35 minutes, until rice is tender and mixture is creamy.
Stir in sugar during the last 10 minutes of cooking, adjusting to taste.
Remove cinnamon stick and lemon zest strips.
Spoon into bowls, dust with ground cinnamon, and serve warm or chilled.

title: Chipirones en su Tinta
shortDescription: Baby squid braised in a deeply savory sauce made with their own ink, a dramatic black dish beloved in the Basque Country.
note: Reserve the ink sacs carefully when cleaning the squid, or use store-bought squid ink packets if fresh ink is unavailable.
introCopy: Chipirones en su tinta is a striking Basque delicacy, tender baby squid simmered in a rich, inky sauce built on a deeply caramelized onion sofrito. It's traditionally served with white rice to soak up the intensely savory sauce.

steps.text: Heat olive oil in a pot; cook onions and pepper very slowly over low heat until deeply softened and caramelized, about 25 minutes.
Add garlic and tomato, cooking until jammy, about 8 minutes.
Pour in wine and simmer 3 minutes, then stir in squid ink dissolved in fish stock.
Add squid bodies and tentacles, season with salt, cover, and simmer gently until tender, about 15-20 minutes.
Serve hot spooned over white rice.

title: Espárragos a la Plancha con Jamón
shortDescription: Griddled green asparagus wrapped with thin slices of Serrano ham, finished with a drizzle of good olive oil.
note: Cook the asparagus just until tender-crisp — overcooking will make it stringy and dull its bright color.
introCopy: This simple tapa pairs quickly griddled asparagus with the salty richness of Serrano ham, a combination found across Spanish tapas menus in springtime when asparagus is at its best.

steps.text: Wrap 2-3 asparagus spears together with a slice of Serrano ham.
Heat olive oil in a griddle pan or skillet over medium-high heat.
Cook the bundles, turning occasionally, until asparagus is tender-crisp and ham is lightly crisped, about 6-8 minutes.
Sprinkle with sea salt and serve immediately, with lemon wedges if desired.

title: Ensaladilla Rusa
shortDescription: A creamy Spanish potato salad with carrots, peas, tuna, and mayonnaise, a beloved tapas bar staple served chilled.
note: Dice the potatoes and carrots into small, even cubes so every bite has a good mix of textures.
introCopy: Despite its name referencing Russian salad, ensaladilla rusa has become thoroughly Spanish, found on tapas menus nationwide. Creamy mayonnaise binds tender potatoes, carrots, peas, and tuna into a comforting, crowd-pleasing dish.

steps.text: Boil potatoes and carrots in salted water until just tender, about 12 minutes; add peas for the final 3 minutes. Drain and cool completely.
In a large bowl, combine cooled potatoes, carrots, peas, tuna, chopped eggs, and olives.
Whisk mayonnaise with vinegar and salt, then fold gently into the vegetable mixture until evenly coated.
Transfer to a serving dish, smooth the top, and garnish with sliced egg.
Refrigerate at least 1 hour before serving chilled.

title: Bacalao a la Vizcaína
shortDescription: Salt cod simmered in a rich, deep red Basque pepper sauce made from dried choricero peppers and a slow-cooked onion sofrito.
note: Rehydrate dried choricero peppers in warm water before scraping out the pulp, which is essential to the sauce's signature color and flavor.
introCopy: Bacalao a la Vizcaína is a treasured dish from the Basque province of Vizcaya, showcasing salt cod in a luxuriously thick red sauce built from choricero peppers. It's traditionally served during the Christmas season.

steps.text: Soak dried choricero peppers in warm water for 30 minutes, then scrape the pulp from the skins with a spoon; discard skins.
Heat olive oil in a pot and cook onions very slowly over low heat until deeply softened, about 25 minutes.
Add garlic and tomato, cooking until jammy, then stir in pepper pulp, toasted bread, and paprika.
Blend the sauce until smooth, adding a little cod poaching liquid or water to loosen, then return to the pot.
Nestle cod pieces into the sauce, cover, and simmer gently until cod is tender and flakes easily, about 12-15 minutes.

title: Sopa de Ajo
shortDescription: A rustic Castilian garlic soup thickened with bread and paprika, topped with a poached egg for a warming, humble meal.
note: Toast the bread and garlic well before adding liquid — this builds the deep, savory base flavor of the soup.
introCopy: Sopa de ajo is classic Castilian peasant food, transforming stale bread, garlic, and paprika into a deeply comforting soup. A poached or lightly cooked egg stirred in at the end turns it into a satisfying full meal.

steps.text: Heat olive oil in a pot over medium heat; cook garlic until fragrant and just golden, about 2 minutes.
Add bread and toast in the oil, stirring, for 3-4 minutes until golden.
Stir in paprika, then immediately pour in stock and salt to prevent the paprika from burning.
Simmer 15 minutes, until bread has broken down and thickened the soup slightly.
Crack eggs directly into the simmering soup and poach 3-4 minutes until whites are set.
Ladle into bowls, ensuring each gets an egg, and garnish with parsley.

title: Migas
shortDescription: Crispy fried breadcrumbs studded with chorizo, pancetta, and garlic, a rustic shepherd's dish from Extremadura and Castile.
note: Let torn bread dry out overnight, or lightly moisten stale bread, so the migas fry up crisp rather than soggy.
introCopy: Migas began as humble shepherd's food, a way to use up stale bread by frying it crisp with whatever meat and garlic was on hand. Today it's a beloved rustic dish, often finished with fried eggs or grapes.

steps.text: Sprinkle torn bread with water, toss to lightly moisten, and let sit 30 minutes covered with a towel.
Heat olive oil in a large skillet; cook pancetta and chorizo until browned and crisp, about 6 minutes. Remove and set aside.
In the same oil, add garlic and cook until fragrant, about 1 minute.
Add moistened bread and paprika, frying over medium heat, stirring and breaking up clumps, until crisp and golden, about 12-15 minutes.
Return meat to the pan, season with salt, and toss to combine. Serve hot, topped with fried eggs or grapes if desired.

title: Solomillo al Whisky
shortDescription: Pan-seared pork tenderloin medallions in a bold garlic, lemon, and whisky pan sauce, a popular Spanish bar and home-cooking favorite.
note: Let the whisky reduce fully to cook off the alcohol, leaving behind a deeply savory, slightly sweet glaze.
introCopy: Solomillo al whisky is a staple on Spanish restaurant menus, combining tender pork medallions with a punchy garlic and whisky sauce. It comes together quickly, making it a favorite for both home cooks and tapas bars alike.

steps.text: Season pork medallions with salt and pepper.
Heat olive oil in a skillet over medium-high heat; sear pork medallions until golden and just cooked through, about 3 minutes per side. Remove and set aside.
Add garlic to the pan and cook until fragrant, about 1 minute.
Carefully add whisky (it may flame briefly) and let reduce by half, scraping up browned bits.
Stir in lemon juice, return pork to the pan, and toss to coat in the sauce.
Sprinkle with parsley and serve immediately with french fries.

title: Pollo al Ajillo
shortDescription: Bone-in chicken pieces browned and braised with abundant garlic cloves, white wine, and sherry until tender and deeply savory.
note: Leave the garlic cloves whole and unpeeled if you like — they turn soft and sweet, perfect for squeezing out onto bread.
introCopy: Pollo al ajillo is a simple, rustic dish found in home kitchens and tavernas throughout Spain. An abundance of garlic mellows into a nutty sweetness as the chicken braises in white wine and a splash of sherry.

steps.text: Season chicken with salt. Heat olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat and brown chicken pieces on all sides, about 10 minutes; remove.
Add garlic cloves to the pan and cook, stirring, until lightly golden, about 3 minutes.
Return chicken to the pan, pour in wine and sherry, add bay leaf, and bring to a simmer.
Cover and cook over low heat until chicken is cooked through and tender, about 20-25 minutes.
Remove bay leaf, sprinkle with parsley, and serve with crusty bread.

title: Habas con Jamón
shortDescription: Tender fava beans braised with Serrano ham, garlic, and mint, a beloved springtime dish from Andalusia and Granada.
note: Fresh young fava beans don't need peeling, but if using larger, older beans, blanch and slip off the tough outer skins first.
introCopy: Habas con jamón celebrates the arrival of spring's first fava beans, gently braised with salty Serrano ham and a whisper of fresh mint. It's a simple, seasonal dish beloved throughout southern Spain.

steps.text: Heat olive oil in a pan and cook onion until soft, about 6 minutes.
Add garlic and ham, cooking until fragrant, about 2 minutes.
Add fava beans, wine, and water; season with salt.
Cover and simmer gently until beans are tender, about 12-15 minutes, adding more water if needed.
Stir in fresh mint just before serving.

title: Sardinas a la Plancha
shortDescription: Whole fresh sardines griddled quickly until crisp-skinned and smoky, finished simply with olive oil, lemon, and flaky salt.
note: Score the skin lightly before cooking to help the sardines cook evenly and prevent curling on the griddle.
introCopy: Sardinas a la plancha is a beloved coastal Spanish tapa, especially popular in summer beach chiringuitos. Fresh sardines need only a hot griddle, good olive oil, and a squeeze of lemon to shine.

steps.text: Pat sardines dry and rub lightly with 1 tablespoon of the olive oil.
Heat a griddle or cast iron pan over high heat until very hot.
Cook sardines in batches, about 2-3 minutes per side, until skin is crisp and flesh is just cooked through.
Arrange on a platter, drizzle with remaining olive oil, sprinkle with sea salt and parsley, and serve immediately with lemon wedges.
